title: How do I fast, and what is Lent for?
seoTitle: How to Fast as a Christian, and What Lent Is For
description: How to fast as a Christian: health cautions first, starting with one meal, what fasting is for, and what Lent, Ash Wednesday, and a Daniel fast mean.
summary: What fasting is for, how to begin safely, what to give up for Lent, and why some churches keep it and others don't.
askedAs: what does the Bible say about fasting
what to give up for Lent
answer: Maybe Lent is coming and you're wondering what to give up, or your church has called a fast, or you want to go without food and pray and don't know where to begin. Start with your health. Talk with a doctor before you fast from food if you've had an eating disorder or a long struggle with food, if you have diabetes or another medical condition or take regular medication, if you're pregnant or nursing or under eighteen, or if fasting has become about your weight or control. You can fast from something else instead; no one is less faithful for it. Otherwise, begin small: skip one meal, keep drinking water, and spend that time with God. Christian fasting is hunger turned toward God. It isn't a diet, a performance, or a way to make God do what you want. Lent is a season for it, the forty days before Easter, kept by many churches and not by others.
happening:
Some people come to fasting carrying something heavy. A child is sick or a marriage is failing, and someone said *fast and pray about it*, and you're willing but don't know how. Others come because the calendar turned: Lent is near, friends are giving up sugar or social media, or your church is starting a season of prayer and fasting. Maybe you've tried before. By midafternoon your head ached, you snapped at someone you love, and when you finally ate you felt less like a saint than a failure. Or maybe you've never heard a sermon on fasting and assumed it was for monks.

The usual explanations each hold some truth. The health explanation, from intermittent fasting to cleanses, says fasting is good for you. Plenty of healthy adults can skip a meal without harm, but for some bodies going without food is a real risk, and if the goal is your weight, it's a diet, however devout it feels. If food has ever been a battle for you, the word itself may set off alarms. Listen to them. The discipline explanation says fasting builds willpower, and it does show you how much of your day runs on small comforts. But discipline aimed at yourself tends to end in pride or despair; in Jesus' story, the man who fasted twice a week wasn't the one who went home justified (Luke 18:12-14).

The spiritual explanation says fasting makes prayer stronger and moves God to act. Scripture does join fasting to prayer, and sometimes God granted what was asked (Ezra 8:23), but it also records a fast he refused (Isaiah 58:3-4). The skeptic calls self-denial superstition, or contempt for the body, and Christians have sometimes given him reason. But the Bible that commends fasting also calls food a good gift, received with thanksgiving (1 Timothy 4:3-4), and it warns that “harsh treatment of the body” is “of no value against the indulgence of the flesh” (Colossians 2:23).

What these explanations leave out is that fasting in Scripture is aimed at someone. It's hunger offered to God, a way of saying with your body what words can't carry: that you're sorry, or grieving, or afraid, or that you want him more than bread. It's done before a Father who sees, and it looks toward a feast.

scripture.intro: The Bible gives no manual for fasting and never says how often Christians should do it. It shows people fasting because they were grieving, or sorry, or in danger, and it shows God refusing a fast that was really a bargain. Read these slowly: Jesus taking fasting for granted, the fast God chooses, a call to come home, and the forty days Lent remembers.

passages.text: When you fast, do not be somber like the hypocrites, for they disfigure their faces to show men they are fasting. Truly I tell you, they already have their full reward. But when you fast, anoint your head and wash your face, so that your fasting will not be obvious to men, but only to your Father, who is unseen. And your Father, who sees what is done in secret, will reward you.
passages.reading: These lines sit in the middle of the Sermon on the Mount, where Jesus takes up three things devout people did: giving, praying, and fasting. Each time he begins with *when*. He assumes his followers will fast. His warning is about the audience. The hypocrites made sure everyone could see their hunger, and Jesus says that attention is all the reward they'll get. Washing and anointing were the ordinary care that mourners and people fasting set aside (2 Samuel 12:20; Daniel 10:3); Jesus tells you to keep them, so the day looks like any other and the fast never becomes a display of suffering. That doesn't forbid telling your husband or wife why you're skipping dinner, or fasting with your church. It means the fast is offered to the Father who sees what no one else sees. Jesus promises that the Father will reward it, but not that the reward will be the thing you were fasting for. That is the Father's to give.

passages.text: “Why have we fasted, and You have not seen? Why have we humbled ourselves, and You have not noticed?” “Behold, on the day of your fast, you do as you please, and you oppress all your workers. ... Isn’t this the fast that I have chosen: to break the chains of wickedness, to untie the cords of the yoke, to set the oppressed free and tear off every yoke? Isn’t it to share your bread with the hungry, to bring the poor and homeless into your home, to clothe the naked when you see him, and not to turn away from your own flesh and blood?
passages.reading: The people in this chapter kept the forms of fasting with care, and they complained that God hadn't noticed. God's answer is blunt: on their fast days they did as they pleased, oppressed their workers, and fasted with quarrels and fists. He asks whether a day of bowing the head like a reed and lying on sackcloth and ashes is the fast he chose (verse 5), then names the fast he did choose, and it faces outward: break the chains, share your bread, take in the homeless, clothe the naked, don't turn away from your own family. The promise comes after: “Then you will call, and the LORD will answer” (verse 9). A fast meant to make God notice us misses the point, and so does a fast that only punishes the one who keeps it. The fast he chose makes us notice the hungry. It's a hard chapter to read with a full pantry.

passages.text: “Yet even now,” declares the LORD, “return to Me with all your heart, with fasting, weeping, and mourning.” So rend your hearts and not your garments, and return to the LORD your God. For He is gracious and compassionate, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion. And He relents from sending disaster.
passages.reading: The book of Joel opens with a plague of locusts that had stripped the land (Joel 1:4), and the prophet calls everyone, old and young, to fast. In that world grief tore its clothes, and God asks for more than the outward sign. Then comes the reason anyone would dare come back: God is described in the words he spoke of himself to Moses at Sinai, gracious and compassionate, slow to anger (Exodus 34:6). Joel stakes everything on that character and leaves the outcome open: “Who knows? He may turn and relent” (verse 14). For anyone coming back to God, that's enough to come home on. Many churches read this passage on Ash Wednesday.

passages.text: Then Jesus was led by the Spirit into the wilderness to be tempted by the devil. After fasting forty days and forty nights, He was hungry. The tempter came to Him and said, “If You are the Son of God, tell these stones to become bread.” But Jesus answered, “It is written: ‘Man shall not live on bread alone, but on every word that comes from the mouth of God.’”
passages.reading: Jesus has just been baptized and heard his Father call him his beloved Son (Matthew 3:17), and the Spirit leads him into the wilderness. Forty days without food recalls Moses on the mountain (Exodus 34:28) and Israel's forty years in the desert. Matthew says simply, “He was hungry.” The tempter's offer sounds reasonable: you're the Son of God, so feed yourself. Jesus answers with Moses' words about the manna, given so a hungry people would learn to live by God's word (Deuteronomy 8:3). Where Israel grumbled, he trusted. Lent's forty days remember his, though no one should try to repeat what he did. It asks us to follow him a little way into the wilderness and find out what we've been living on.

whyHard:
The usual explanation for why fasting feels impossible is abundance. For many of us food waits in the cupboard, and a phone can answer almost any craving within the hour. A person who rarely waits for anything finds it strange to wait on purpose. That's true, and it matters. But it can't be the whole story, because the people of Isaiah 58 lived with nothing like our plenty and still turned their fasting into a quarrel and a bargain. Fasting bends easily back toward ourselves.

In our day it bends two ways. The wellness story sells fasting as a tool for a leaner body or a longer life. The transaction story treats it as a way to move God: give up food for twenty-one days and expect your breakthrough. One sounds secular and the other devout, but they share a grammar, and both make fasting a way of getting. Scripture's fasting speaks differently. When David fasted for his dying son, when Joel called his people to fast, and when the king of Nineveh sat in ashes, each said the same two words: “Who knows?” (2 Samuel 12:22; Joel 2:14; Jonah 3:9). That's what humility sounds like when it asks. Pastors, and I'm one of them, have reason to prefer the transaction story, because a fast with a promise attached is easier to preach than hunger offered to God with no guarantee.

The church has known both the gift and the bend for a long time. The Didache, one of the oldest Christian writings outside the New Testament, tells believers to fast on Wednesdays and Fridays and before a baptism. Near the end of the second century, when Victor, the bishop of Rome, tried to cut off the churches of Asia Minor over the date of Easter, Irenaeus of Lyon reminded him that Christians fasted before Easter in different ways, some for a day, some for two or more, and that the difference in the fast only confirmed their agreement in the faith. By the fourth century many churches kept a forty-day fast before Easter, a season closely tied to preparing converts for baptism, and the church fasted with them. Over the centuries those fasts hardened into rules, and the Reformers came to believe that keeping the rules had become a way of earning standing with God. In Lent of 1522 the Zurich printer Christoph Froschauer served sausages in his house, and Huldrych Zwingli, the preacher at the city's Grossmünster, defended those who ate them in a sermon on Christian freedom in food. The Reformers didn't reject fasting itself. In the 1640s the Westminster Assembly, which held that no day but the Lord's Day was to be kept holy, still wrote directions for days of public fasting. Many who inherited their freedom, though, let the fast slip away.

Underneath all of this is the reason Jesus gave. His disciples didn't fast while he was with them, because no one fasts at a wedding, but the time would come when the bridegroom was taken from them, and then they would fast (Mark 2:19-20). Christian fasting belongs to the time we live in now, between his going and his coming. It's what love does in an absence, the body's way of praying “Come, Lord Jesus” (Revelation 22:20). That's why it comes so hard to comfortable people, and I count myself among them. Our trouble isn't mainly willpower. We've stopped noticing that anything is missing. But a hunger you never let yourself feel is still a hunger, and the people Isaiah 58 told us to feed are still hungry. The bridegroom is still away. Fasting asks whether we miss him.

thisWeek.intro: You don't need to start with forty days, or even a whole day. Start with one meal and let the hunger do what it's for. If food is complicated for you, the first step may be the only one you need, and a fast from something else is a real fast.

steps.title: Check your health first
steps.body: Before you fast from food, talk with a doctor if you've had an eating disorder or a long struggle with food, if you have diabetes or another medical condition or take regular medication, if you're pregnant or nursing or under eighteen, or if fasting has become about weight or control. Meanwhile, or instead, fast from something else: your phone for an evening, a show, the news. No one is less faithful for that. Even the Roman Catholic Church, which requires most adults to fast on two days a year, excuses the sick and women who are pregnant or nursing. This page isn't medical advice.

steps.title: Skip one meal, and keep drinking water
steps.body: Choose one meal this week (lunch is a common place to start) and don't eat it. Keep drinking water; going without water isn't safe, and a beginner's fast never calls for it. Expect hunger, maybe a headache or a short temper. If you feel faint, dizzy, or unwell, eat something, and don't call it failure. Break the fast gently with a modest, ordinary meal, and give thanks; don't make it a reward or a binge. And keep it quiet: Jesus told those who fast to wash their faces (Matthew 6:17).

steps.title: Spend the time with God
steps.body: The hunger is meant to send you somewhere. Use the time you'd have spent eating: pray the Lord's Prayer slowly, read a psalm, or read a chapter of Mark. When hunger comes back, answer it with one sentence: *I want you more than this.* If you're not sure how to begin, see the page for when [you don't know how to pray](/help/prayer).

steps.title: Give away what you would have spent
steps.body: In the second century, a Christian book called the Shepherd of Hermas told believers to add up what their food would have cost on a fast day and give it to a widow, an orphan, or someone in need. Do the same. Give the price of your skipped meal to a food pantry, a struggling neighbor, or your church's fund for the hungry. That's the fast God chose: “to share your bread with the hungry” (Isaiah 58:7).

steps.title: If Lent is near, choose a fast and a practice
steps.body: In Western churches Lent begins on Ash Wednesday, forty-six days before Easter. Choose one thing to give up that you'll miss every day, food or not, and one thing to take up. The site's printable [Forty Days With Mark](/plans#lent-with-mark) reading plan walks through Mark from Ash Wednesday to Easter morning, a few scenes a day. Sundays aren't counted in the forty, and many people set their fast aside on them. If your church holds an Ash Wednesday service, go; if not, read Joel 2 and Psalm 51 that morning.

moreHelp.body:
Many questions about fasting are for a pastor or a friend who prays. Some are for a doctor: before you fast from food if the health cautions on this page fit you, before any fast longer than a day, and right away if fasting leaves you faint, confused, or with a racing heart. If you've had an eating disorder, bring whoever treated you into that decision. Some questions are for a counselor. If you're fasting to lose weight and calling it devotion, fasting to feel in control, hiding how little you eat, eating in secret after a fast, or feeling you must go without to be acceptable to God, that deserves care from someone trained for it.

If you drink heavily every day, talk with a doctor before you give it up for Lent, because stopping suddenly can bring on a dangerous withdrawal. And if giving it up shows you that you can't stop, take that seriously; the page for when [you can't stop drinking or using](/help/addiction) can help, and the help lines at the end of this page include one for drinking and drugs. If a church or leader pressures people to fast beyond what's safe, or shames those who can't, that's a misuse of spiritual authority; talk with someone you trust outside that group.

To find a counselor, ask your doctor for a referral, check your insurer's directory, or ask a pastor which counselors nearby they trust. If food is part of the struggle, ask for someone experienced with eating disorders. If you want a Christian counselor, say so; either way, check that they're licensed in your state.
signs: You have diabetes or another medical condition, take regular medication, have struggled with eating, are pregnant or nursing, or are under eighteen. See your doctor before fasting from food.
While fasting you feel faint, confused, or very weak, or your heart races. Stop and eat, and get medical help if it doesn't pass. For chest pain, call 911.
You're fasting to lose weight, to feel in control, or to punish yourself, hiding how little you eat, or ending fasts by eating in secret. Talk with a doctor or counselor.
Food, weight, or the next fast fills most of your thoughts, or eating leaves you ashamed. Talk with a doctor or counselor.
You feel you must fast more and more to be forgiven by God, and nothing is ever enough. Talk with a counselor as well as a pastor.
Giving something up for Lent has shown you that you can't stop drinking or using, or stopping has left you shaking or sick. See a doctor; for a seizure or hallucinations, call 911.
You have thoughts of ending your life, or of not wanting to be alive. Call or text 988 now, or 911 if you're in danger.
moreHelp.firstCall: To your doctor: *I'd like to fast for religious reasons, maybe one meal a week or a partial fast during Lent. Here are my conditions and medicines. Is it safe for me, and what should I watch for?* If eating has been hard for you: *I've struggled with food before, and I want to be careful. Is fasting wise for me?* To a counselor: *I started fasting for my faith, and I think it's turned into something else.*
moreHelp.cost: A question for your doctor may cost no more than a message through your patient portal or a few minutes at your next visit. A pastor costs nothing. For counseling, ask about sliding-scale fees, look for a community mental health center or a university training clinic, and check whether your employer offers an employee assistance program, which often covers a few sessions. Some churches keep a benevolence fund to help, and it's fine to ask.

helping.body:
Maybe your teenager wants to join the youth group's fast, or your husband or wife has started skipping meals and calling it a fast, or you lead a group planning a church-wide fast. Start with care for the body. A child or teenager who wants to fast should talk with a doctor first, and can fast from something other than food: a phone, a game, a favorite show. If someone you love has struggled with eating, don't encourage a food fast, and watch gently for the signs above. If you're worried that someone's fasting has become something else, talk with them alone, kindly and plainly, about what you've seen, and help them get to a doctor.

If you lead, keep it voluntary and quiet. Offer ways to fast that don't involve food, and say from the front that no one is less faithful for choosing them. Don't promise what a fast will get, don't count who's fasting, and don't let anyone be shamed for eating. When the fast ends, eat together.
say: You don't have to fast from food to keep Lent.
Want to skip lunch together on Wednesday and pray?
If you feel sick, eat something. God isn't keeping score.
I've noticed you're skipping a lot of meals. Can we talk?
Let's give what we would have spent to someone who's hungry.
dontSay: If you really wanted an answer, you'd fast.
It's not a real fast unless it's food.
At least you'll lose a few pounds.
helping.next: Fast with them once, simply, and eat together afterward. For a family, [How to Keep Lent and Easter as a Family](/how-tos/fam-how-to-keep-lent-and-easter-as-a-family) has ideas that work with children. For a group, [Spiritual Habits: A Bible Study on Formation](/studyguides/habits-and-formation) takes up fasting among the church's disciplines. If you see the signs above, help the person call a doctor or counselor, and offer to go along.

prayer:
Father, I'm hungry for a lot of things, and most of them aren't you. I reach for food, and my phone, and anything else that keeps me from feeling what's missing. You know how I'm made. You remember that I am dust.

Your Son went hungry in the wilderness and trusted your word more than bread. I can't do what he did, and I'm not trying to impress you. Let this small hunger turn me toward you, and when it bites, remind me that I don't live on bread alone.

Keep me from fasting to be seen, or to strike a bargain. I don't know what you'll do with what I'm asking. Who knows? But you are gracious and compassionate, slow to anger, and that's reason enough to come home.

Let what I don't eat feed someone who is hungry and didn't choose it. And while the Bridegroom is away, don't let me get used to his absence.

Come, Lord Jesus. Amen.

Why Would Anyone Give Something Up for Lent?

faq.a: Jesus assumed his followers would fast. He says “When you fast” (Matthew 6:16) as he says “when you pray” (Matthew 6:5), and he said his disciples would fast once the bridegroom was taken from them (Mark 2:20). The leaders of the church at Antioch were “worshiping the Lord and fasting” when the Spirit set apart Barnabas and Saul (Acts 13:2). But the New Testament sets no rule for how often or how long, and no one earns God's favor by going hungry. Jesus expects fasting more than he commands it, and if your health rules out going without food, you can fast from something else.

Start with one meal. When that's familiar, try a full day, from one evening meal to the next, drinking water throughout. Scripture shows fasts that lasted a day “until evening” (Judges 20:26), three days without food or water when Esther's people faced death (Esther 4:16), and three weeks of plain food (Daniel 10:2-3). Esther's fast and the forty-day fasts of Moses and Jesus belong to singular moments in God's story, and they aren't patterns to copy: never go without water, and talk with a doctor before any fast longer than a day. A short fast kept honestly is worth more than a long one kept for show.

faq.q: What is Lent, and do I have to keep it?
faq.a: Lent is the forty days before Easter, beginning in Western churches on Ash Wednesday, with Sundays, traditionally feast days, left out of the count. Its forty days remember Jesus in the wilderness. The Bible never commands it; it grew in the early church, closely tied to preparing converts for baptism at Easter. The Roman Catholic Church asks most adults to fast on Ash Wednesday and Good Friday; many churches mark the season and leave the fast to each person; others don't keep it. Those who keep it receive the church year as a gift, a yearly walk through Christ's life, and say a season can teach without saving anyone: “He who observes a special day does so to the Lord” (Romans 14:6). Those who don't keep it hold that believers are free of any season Scripture doesn't command, and have seen a church's custom harden into a law or turn into a show; the letter to the Colossians tells believers not to let anyone judge them by what they eat “or with regard to a feast” (Colossians 2:16). To both, Paul says neither may look down on or judge the other, “for God has accepted him” (Romans 14:3).

faq.q: What should I give up for Lent?
faq.a: Choose something you'll miss every day, so its absence keeps reminding you why: a meal, meat, sweets, alcohol, social media, a nightly show. Don't give up a sin for Lent; give that up for good. Don't choose anything that would harm you or the people who depend on you. If food is hard for you, fast from something else, and if you drink heavily every day, talk with a doctor before you stop. Many people also take something up: a daily reading, such as the site's [Forty Days With Mark](/plans#lent-with-mark) plan, a time of prayer, or a gift to the hungry from what they save. Let the empty place turn you toward God.

It's the first day of Lent in Western churches. In many of them a minister marks each forehead with ash, often in the sign of a cross, with words drawn from Genesis 3:19: “For dust you are, and to dust you shall return.” The ash is customarily made by burning the previous year's palm branches. In Scripture, ashes went with grief and repentance (Daniel 9:3; Jonah 3:6). Some Christians think the practice sits uneasily with Jesus' warning not to show your fasting (Matthew 6:16-18), often read that day. Those who keep it answer that the ash is a shared confession, not a display of devotion: everyone in line is mortal and needs mercy.

It's a partial fast, often kept for twenty-one days, of vegetables, fruit, grains, and water, without meat, sweets, or wine. It's a popular practice, not a biblical command, and the Bible never uses the name, but it draws on two passages. In Daniel 1, Daniel and his friends asked for vegetables and water rather than defile themselves with the king's food, which was faithfulness in exile more than a fast. In Daniel 10, Daniel “was mourning for three full weeks” and “ate no rich food, no meat or wine” (Daniel 10:2-3). That fast was grief and humility before God, and the messenger who came told him his words had been heard “from the first day” (Daniel 10:12), before the three weeks were done. A partial fast can be a wise way to begin; if the health cautions here apply to you, ask your doctor first.

slots.note: James came to faith from atheism. He could add, in his own words, how fasting and Lent looked to him from outside the church, and what his first fast was like, if he has kept one. The second pass cut a sentence that used his atheism to say he understands the person who is sure nothing is missing, because it described his inner life before faith; the section ends without it. The linked essay Why Christians Fast narrates a first fast in the first person: if that story is his, this is the place for it in his words; if it isn't, the essay needs correcting.

Where James lands on keeping Lent and on Ash Wednesday ashes, in his own words, and why. The answer to What is Lent, and do I have to keep it? gives the case for keeping it (the church year as a gift, Romans 14:6) and the case against (freedom from seasons Scripture doesn't command, and the worry that custom becomes a law or a show, Colossians 2:16), with Romans 14:3 to both, and deliberately does not land; the Ash Wednesday answer states both views of ashes and Matthew 6 without a verdict.

On Matthew 6:16-18: James was raised without a father. He could add, in his own words, what it means to him that Jesus grounds fasting in a Father who sees what no one else sees, and what raising five sons has taught him about being seen. The reading stands without it.
James's own practice of fasting as a pastor (how often, what he does with the time and the money saved), if he is willing to share it, as one real example beside the five steps.
Whether and how James's household keeps Lent or fasts with his sons, in his own words, beside the guidance for parents. Only from James; nothing has been written for him.

sources.claim: The Didache tells Christians to fast on Wednesdays and Fridays (8.1), and tells the one baptizing, the one being baptized, and any others who can to fast beforehand (7.4).

sources.claim: When Victor, bishop of Rome, tried to cut off the churches of Asia over the date of Easter, Irenaeus of Lyon wrote to him that Christians fasted before Easter for different lengths (one day, two, more, or forty hours) and that the disagreement in the fast confirmed the agreement in the faith.
sources.cite: Eusebius, Church History 5.24 (Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Series 2, Vol. 1), Sacred Texts edition

sources.claim: A forty-day fast before Easter is attested by the fourth century (canon 5 of the Council of Nicaea, 325, already speaks of the forty days) and is closely tied to the preparation of candidates for baptism at Easter; because Sunday was not a fast day, the forty days are counted without Sundays.

In Lent of 1522 sausages were served and eaten at the Zurich house of the printer Christoph Froschauer, and Huldrych Zwingli, then the people's priest (preacher) at the Grossmünster, defended the eating in a sermon on the choice and freedom of foods.
sources.cite: World History Encyclopedia, Zwingli's On Rejecting Lent and Protecting Christian Liberty

sources.claim: The Westminster Assembly's Directory for the Public Worship of God holds that no day but the Lord's Day is commanded to be kept holy and that festival days are not to be continued, and it includes directions for days of public solemn fasting.
sources.cite: The Directory for the Publick Worship of God (1645), Of Publick Solemn Fasting and the Appendix touching Days and Places for Publick Worship

sources.claim: The Shepherd of Hermas tells those who fast to reckon up the price of the food they would have eaten that day and give it to a widow, an orphan, or someone in want.
sources.cite: The Shepherd of Hermas, Similitude 5, chapter 3 (Ante-Nicene Fathers, Vol. 2)

sources.claim: Catholics in the United States aged 18 to 59 are obliged to fast on Ash Wednesday and Good Friday; the physically or mentally ill, including people with chronic illnesses such as diabetes, and pregnant or nursing women are excused.
sources.cite: United States Conference of Catholic Bishops, Fast and Abstinence

sources.claim: The Revised Common Lectionary appoints Joel 2:1-2, 12-17 (or Isaiah 58:1-12) and Matthew 6:1-6, 16-21 for Ash Wednesday.
sources.cite: Revised Common Lectionary, Ash Wednesday (Vanderbilt Divinity Library)

sources.claim: The ashes for Ash Wednesday are customarily made by burning the previous year's Palm Sunday branches, and the words spoken at their imposition are drawn from Genesis 3:19.
sources.cite: National Catholic Register (CNA), Where Do Ash Wednesday Ashes Come From?

sources.claim: Alcohol withdrawal may quickly become life-threatening, especially with delirium tremens; call 911 or go to the emergency room for seizures, fever, severe confusion, or hallucinations.

reviewed.notes: Second-pass edit, done in full from the top (2026-10-01). Validator clean (node scripts/validate-needs.mjs fasting, 4,490 words); the CarePage render test passes for /help/fasting.
